The nightly backup job started failing silently after the storage volume was resized. The script checked the exit code of the archive step but not of the upload, so every night it reported success while the bucket received nothing. We only noticed when someone tried to restore a table that had been dropped by mistake and found the latest usable archive was eleven days old. The fix was small: propagate the upload status, fail the job loudly, and add an alert when the newest object in the bucket is older than thirty hours. The lesson is broader. A job that reports its own success is not evidence of anything; the evidence is the artifact sitting where the consumer expects it, with a timestamp you can read from outside.
---
My grandmother made bread every Saturday morning in a kitchen that was always slightly too cold. She never measured the flour; she poured it from the sack into a chipped enamel bowl until the dough stopped sticking to her palms. The starter lived in a glass jar on the windowsill and had a name nobody remembers anymore. She would cover the bowl with a wool scarf and leave it near the stove while she fed the chickens. By noon the loaves were cooling on the table and the whole house smelled of crust and woodsmoke. I have tried to repeat it many times with a proper scale and a thermometer, and the bread is good, but it is never the same bread.
---
Decision: the public API keeps cursor pagination and drops offset pagination in the next major version. Offset queries on the events table degrade linearly once a workspace passes a few hundred thousand rows, and we measured p95 latency above two seconds for page fifty on the largest tenant. Cursor pagination keeps every page at constant cost because it seeks on the indexed created_at and id pair. Clients that need random access to a page number can still build it on their side by walking the cursors once and caching them. The migration guide must show both the old and the new request shape, and the deprecated parameter keeps working for one release with a warning header so integrators have time to switch.
---
The ferry from the mainland leaves twice a day in summer and once a day in winter, and the winter boat is often cancelled when the wind turns north. The island has one shop, one church, a lighthouse that has been automatic since the seventies, and roughly forty permanent residents. Most of them keep sheep. There is no hotel, but the woman who runs the shop rents two rooms above it, and she will cook dinner if you ask before three in the afternoon. Walking the whole coastline takes about five hours. The western cliffs are where the puffins nest from May to August, and if you sit very still at the edge they come close enough that you can hear their wings.
---
We traced the memory leak in the worker pool to a map that cached compiled templates by their source string. The cache never evicted anything, and one customer generated templates dynamically with a timestamp embedded in the text, so every request produced a new key. Heap profiles showed the map growing by roughly forty megabytes per hour on that node and nowhere else, which is why the aggregate dashboards looked flat. We replaced the map with a bounded LRU keyed by a hash of the normalized template, added a metric for cache size and evictions, and wrote a test that renders ten thousand unique templates and asserts the resident size stays under a fixed ceiling.
---
The chess club meets on Thursday evenings in the back room of the library. Membership is free, and the boards and clocks belong to the club, so you only need to bring yourself. Beginners usually play each other for the first few weeks, and then one of the older members offers to go over their games afterwards. That review is the real lesson: someone patiently pointing at the move where the position started to slip, and asking what you were thinking at that moment. Once a month there is a rapid tournament with fifteen minutes per player, and the winner gets nothing except the right to choose the biscuits for the next meeting, which is taken surprisingly seriously.
---
Runbook for rotating the database credentials of the reporting service. First create the new role with the same grants as the old one and confirm it can connect from the application host. Then update the secret in the vault and restart the service instances one at a time, watching the connection error rate after each restart. Only when every instance has been running on the new role for at least an hour do you revoke the old role. Never revoke first: the service caches connections and a revoked role fails on the next reconnect, which might happen at three in the morning. Record the rotation date in the ops log, together with the command that restores the previous role if something goes wrong.
---
Tomatoes need more sun than most people think. The plants on the north side of our garden produced leaves, plenty of leaves, and almost no fruit, while the same variety two metres away against the south wall was so heavy with fruit that the stakes bent. Watering matters too, but less than consistency: letting the soil dry out completely and then flooding it is what cracks the skins. This year we mulched with straw, watered every second evening, and pinched out the side shoots once a week. We also planted basil between the rows, mostly because it is useful in the kitchen, although the neighbour insists it keeps the whiteflies away. The harvest was the best in five years.

The flaky end-to-end test turned out to be a real race, not a slow environment. The test created a project, immediately created a task in it, and then queried the board. Most of the time the board query ran after the search index caught up; occasionally it ran before, and the task was missing. Retrying the assertion hid the problem for months. The actual bug was in the product: the board endpoint read from the index while the create endpoint returned as soon as the database commit finished, so a real user could see the same gap on a fast connection. We changed the board to read from the primary table for the first page and kept the index for search only.
---
In the spring of 1912 the town council voted to build a covered market on the site of the old cattle yard. The architect was a young engineer from the capital who had never designed anything larger than a railway station waiting room, and the council minutes record a long argument about whether the iron roof would survive the winter snows. It did. The market opened two years later, a few weeks before the war, and for decades it was the busiest place in town on Wednesdays and Saturdays. In the seventies a supermarket opened on the ring road and the stalls emptied one by one. The building was saved from demolition by a petition and now houses a weekend flea market and a small museum of local trades.

Postmortem summary. For forty minutes on Tuesday the login page returned errors for about a third of users. A configuration change meant to raise the session timeout was applied to the wrong environment variable, which the authentication proxy interpreted as a malformed duration and refused to start on the instances that picked up the new config. The health check only verified that the port was open, so the load balancer kept sending traffic to instances where the proxy was crash looping behind a static fallback page. Follow-ups: validate configuration at deploy time, make the health check perform a real token exchange, and add a canary stage that holds the rollout until the error rate on the canary is compared with the baseline.
---
Learning to swim as an adult is mostly about unlearning panic. The body floats much better than you expect once you stop holding your breath and lifting your head to look for the wall. My instructor spent the first two lessons on nothing but breathing: exhale slowly into the water, turn the head, inhale, repeat, while holding the edge of the pool. It felt ridiculous. By the third lesson I could glide a few metres face down without grabbing anything, and by the end of the course I swam a full length of freestyle, slowly and badly, but without stopping. The surprising part was how tired the shoulders get, and how quickly that fades after a few weeks.
---
The queue consumer acknowledged messages before processing them, which made throughput look excellent and lost data whenever a pod was killed during a deploy. We discovered it while reconciling invoice counts between two systems: the downstream ledger was consistently short by a few dozen records per day, always clustered around release times. Switching to acknowledge after successful processing exposed a second problem, because some handlers were not idempotent and a redelivered message created duplicate rows. We added an idempotency key derived from the message identifier, a unique index on it, and a dead letter queue for messages that fail five times. The daily reconciliation now matches exactly.
---
Our rule for code review comments: say what is wrong, why it matters, and what would make it right. A comment that only says that something looks off forces the author to guess, and the guess is usually defensive. A blocking comment must be marked as blocking, so the author knows which remarks they may ignore. Reviewers should report every blocking issue they can see in one pass rather than drip feeding them across rounds, because each round costs a pipeline and a context switch on both sides. Praise is allowed and encouraged when something is genuinely clever or clean. Style preferences that the linter does not enforce are not blocking, however strongly the reviewer feels about them.
---
The old mill on the river has been converted into a small hydroelectric plant run by a cooperative of twelve families. The wheel was replaced with a modern turbine in 2015, but the stone building, the sluice gates and the millpond are original. On an average day it produces enough electricity for the village school and about thirty houses, and surplus power is sold to the grid. The cooperative publishes its accounts on a noticeboard outside the shop. Maintenance is done by volunteers on the first Saturday of each month, and the hardest job is clearing branches and plastic from the intake grid after storms. Visitors can tour the plant in summer if they phone a day ahead.
---
Measured the cold start of the mobile app on three mid range Android phones. The median time to first interactive screen was 4.1 seconds, almost half of which went to initializing an analytics library synchronously on the main thread before anything was drawn. Deferring it until after the first frame cut the median to 2.6 seconds with no loss of events, because the library buffers calls made before initialization. The next largest item was decoding a large splash image at full resolution; serving a properly sized asset saved another 300 milliseconds. We added a startup trace to the release checklist so that a regression above three seconds blocks the build instead of being discovered in store reviews.
---
The museum's collection of maps begins with a hand drawn chart of the harbour from the late sixteenth century, made by a pilot who wanted to warn ships about a sandbar that moved with every storm. The sandbar is drawn three times on the same sheet, in different inks, as if he kept correcting it over the years. Later maps are printed, more confident and less useful. The curator told us that sailors trusted the old pilot's chart long after official surveys existed, because it showed where the danger had been, not only where it was on the day of the survey. The room is dimly lit to protect the paper, and you are given a small torch at the entrance.
---
Incident note: the search service started returning stale results after a schema change added a new column to the documents table. The indexer used SELECT star into a struct with positional scanning, so the new column shifted every field by one and the title went into the body slot. Nothing crashed, because every type still matched by accident. The fix was to list columns explicitly in every query that scans into a struct, and we added a lint rule forbidding SELECT star in repository code. We also reindexed all documents updated during the four hour window. A useful side effect: the explicit column lists made it obvious which queries fetched large text fields they never used.
---
Running a half marathon at forty was harder than I expected and easier than I feared. The plan was twelve weeks: three short runs during the week and one long run on Sunday, increasing by about a kilometre each week, with every fourth week easier to let the legs recover. The long runs were the boring part, two hours alone on the river path, so I started listening to audiobooks and finished four of them before race day. On the day I went out too fast, as everyone warns you not to, and paid for it after the fifteenth kilometre. I still finished in just under two hours, which was the goal, and walked very carefully down stairs for the next three days.
---
The feature flag service must never become a hard dependency of request handling. If it is slow or unavailable, every flag evaluates to its compiled default, and the application logs one warning per minute rather than one per request. Flags are fetched in the background every thirty seconds and kept in memory; a request never waits for the network. Each flag carries an owner and an expiry date, and a weekly job opens a cleanup ticket for flags past their expiry. This policy came out of an outage where the flag service went down and took checkout with it, because one code path evaluated a flag synchronously with no timeout and no default. That path no longer exists.
---
The village orchestra rehearses in the school gym on Monday nights, and anyone who can read music and owns an instrument is welcome. The violins are always plentiful and the brass section is always short of a tuba. The conductor is a retired music teacher who insists on starting exactly at seven and will not tolerate phones on the music stands. Twice a year they give a concert in the church: one at Christmas, one in early summer. The programme is ambitious for an amateur group, often a symphony that is slightly beyond them, and the result is uneven and moving. The audience is mostly relatives, and they applaud between movements, which the conductor has given up correcting.
---
Rate limiting for the public webhooks endpoint is per integration, not per IP address. Several large customers send traffic through a shared corporate proxy, and an IP based limit would let one noisy integration starve all the others behind the same address. Each integration gets a token bucket of sixty requests per minute with a burst of one hundred twenty, and a response over the limit carries a Retry-After header with the number of seconds until the bucket refills. We return status 429 rather than silently dropping requests so that well behaved clients back off. The limits are stored in Redis with a short expiry, and if Redis is unavailable the endpoint allows traffic rather than failing closed.
---
We spent a week in the mountains in October, just after the tourist season ended. Half the huts were already closed, and the ones still open had a single warden cooking soup for whoever turned up. The weather changed every few hours: bright sun in the morning, fog rolling up the valley by lunch, and on two nights a light snowfall that melted by ten the next day. The trails were empty. We saw chamois almost every day, a golden eagle once, and on the last morning a fox walked straight past our tent without looking at us. The descent took longer than planned because the lower path was flooded, and we reached the bus stop ten minutes after the last bus had left.
---
Tried three approaches to deduplicating customer records imported from the old CRM. Exact matching on email found barely half the duplicates because many records had typos or different capitalization. Fuzzy matching on name plus phone produced too many false positives among family members sharing a landline. What worked was a two stage process: normalize emails and phone numbers to a canonical form, group candidates that share either value, and then score each group on name similarity and address overlap, sending anything between the two thresholds to a human review queue. About four percent of records went to review, and the reviewers rejected roughly one in five of the proposed merges.
---
The bakery on the corner closes at two in the afternoon, which seems strange until you learn that the baker starts work at three in the morning. He took over the shop from his father, who took it over from his own father, and the oven is still the original brick one, rebuilt twice but never replaced. The rye loaf is the reason people queue on Saturdays: dense, slightly sour, with caraway seeds and a crust that cracks when you press it. He refuses to sell it sliced. In the window there is a faded photograph of the shop in 1938, with a horse and cart outside and three men in white aprons standing in the doorway, and if you ask he will tell you which one was his grandfather.
